# nish/net/postgres-async

`PgAsyncPool`, PostgreSQL connections an `async` task awaits a query on, so a task's query waits on its socket while the executor runs the others.

```ts
import {
  PG_ASYNC_MAX_SIZE,
  PgAsyncParams,
  PgAsyncPool,
  PgAsyncResult,
  pgAsyncClaim,
  pgAsyncConnect,
  pgAsyncQuery,
  pgAsyncRelease,
} from "nish/net/postgres-async";
```

<scalar-code-group>

```ts example.ts
import { spawn } from "nish:async"
import { secret, wipe } from "nish:secret"
import { PgConfig, pgTarget } from "nish/net/postgres"
import {
  PgAsyncParams, PgAsyncPool, pgAsyncClaim, pgAsyncConnect, pgAsyncQuery, pgAsyncRelease,
} from "nish/net/postgres-async"

async function title(pool: PgAsyncPool, id: i32): Promise<void> {
  const ticket: i32 = await pgAsyncClaim(pool)
  if (ticket < 0) {
    return  // no live connection, or none came free in time
  }
  const params = new PgAsyncParams()
  params.int(id)
  const r = await pgAsyncQuery(pool, ticket, "select title from article where id = $1", params)
  pgAsyncRelease(pool, ticket, r.reusable)
  if (r.ok() && r.rows > 0) {
    console.log(r.text(0, 0))
  }
}

export async function main(): Promise<i32> {
  const config = new PgConfig()
  config.user = "app"
  const pool = new PgAsyncPool(4)
  const password = secret(passwordBytes())  // the program's own source
  const live: i32 = await pgAsyncConnect(pool, config, password, pgTarget("127.0.0.1", 5432))
  wipe(password)
  spawn(title(pool, 1))
  spawn(title(pool, 2))
  // ... and close the pool once the tasks are done: `pool.close()`.
  return live === pool.size ? 0 : 1
}
```

</scalar-code-group>

<scalar-detail title="Why three calls">

A spawned task shares the pool with the function that
spawned it, and runs in memory of its own that is freed when it ends
(docs/LANGUAGE.md → "What `spawn` may pass"). So a call that writes into
the pool may allocate nothing, and one that allocates may not write into
it: `pgAsyncClaim` and `pgAsyncRelease` write only numbers into the pool,
and `pgAsyncQuery` only reads it, building its buffers, rows and strings in
the task's own memory. One `async` function doing all three would be
refused when a task calls it ("hands `pool` to ..., which may grow it").

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="The flow">

`pgAsyncConnect`, in `main` or any function that is not a
spawned task, connects each slot and runs its startup and SCRAM exchange
on a `PgConnection`, which then wipes the password and is dropped: the
pool keeps only the authenticated socket, so it holds no `Secret` and a
task may be handed it. `pgAsyncClaim` gives a task a ticket for one free
connection; `pgAsyncQuery` writes Parse, Bind, Execute and Sync in one go
(the parameters in text, never spliced into the SQL), waits on `writable`
and `readable` for the socket while the executor runs the others, and reads
to the ReadyForQuery; `pgAsyncRelease` gives the connection back, or closes
it when the query left it unfit to reuse.

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="Claiming">

When every live connection is claimed, `pgAsyncClaim` sleeps
and looks again, 1 ms then doubling to 16 ms, until one is free or it has
slept `claimWaitMs` in all; a released connection is not announced, so a
waiter finds it on its next look. A ticket names a slot and that slot's
claim: `pgAsyncQuery` and `pgAsyncRelease` panic on one that is not the
slot's current claim, so two tasks never share a connection and a
connection is given back once.

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="Reuse">

A connection is given back only when its last query read to a
ReadyForQuery that says "idle" and changed no session setting: a query that
left a transaction open, a `SET` the server reported (a ParameterStatus),
a socket error, a frame this module does not expect, or a reply past a cap
closes it, so the next task never inherits another's session.

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-callout type="warning">

**Limits.** `PgAsyncPool`'s caps (`maxMessage`, `maxColumns`, `maxRows`,
`claimWaitMs`) bound what one query keeps; rows past `maxRows` are read
and dropped, and the query fails with `PG_ERR_TOO_BIG`. There is no
deadline on a wait: a server that accepts and never answers holds the task
(and, in `pgAsyncConnect`, the caller) until it closes; bound a slow
statement with the server's `statement_timeout`.

</scalar-callout>

<scalar-detail title="Memory">

Run each query in a spawned task, as `title` does above: the
task's region, and every buffer, row and string the query built in it,
is freed when the task ends, so `Arena.used()` stays where it was across
thousands of queries. A query awaited outside a task, through a function
that is handed the pool, keeps what it built until an enclosing scope
ends (about 9 KB a query, measured while writing
`tests/link/std_postgres_async_flat`).

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="Errors">

A query answers `PG_CARRIER_DONE`, or `PG_CARRIER_FAILED` with
`failure` a `PG_ERR_*` and `socketError` a negative errno, as
`nish/net/postgres-carrier` does: `PG_ERR_NONE` when the server refused the
statement (`errorCode` and `errorMessage` say why, and the connection is
reused), `PG_ERR_CLOSED` when the socket ended or a wait could not be made.
Programming errors (a ticket that is not a current claim, a size out of
range) panic.

</scalar-detail>

`tests/link/std_postgres_async` runs one against a loopback backend;
`tests/link/std_postgres_async_flat` reads `Arena.used()` across thousands
of queries. Caps and findings: `docs/security/postgres.md`.

Written for this module; not ported from another implementation.

## Functions

### pgAsyncClaim

Claims a free connection for the calling task, sleeping while every live
one is claimed: 1 ms, then twice as long each time up to 16 ms, for at most
`pool.claimWaitMs` in all. It writes only numbers into the pool, so a
spawned task may call it.

```ts
function pgAsyncClaim(
  pool: PgAsyncPool,
): Promise<i32>
```

<scalar-field name="pool" type="PgAsyncPool" required>

The pool.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="returns" type="Promise&lt;i32&gt;">

A ticket (0 or more) for `pgAsyncQuery` and then exactly one
  `pgAsyncRelease`; `-1` (`PG_POOL_NONE`) when no slot is connected;
  `PG_CARRIER_FULL` (-2) when none came free in time.

</scalar-field>

### pgAsyncConnect

Connects every slot of `pool` that is not connected, one after another,
and authenticates each on a `PgConnection` (startup, then SCRAM-SHA-256 or
`trust`), which wipes its copy of the password once the proof is made and
is then dropped. Call it from `main` or another function that is not a
spawned task: it holds the password. A slot that fails stays unconnected;
call it again to retry.

```ts
function pgAsyncConnect(
  pool: PgAsyncPool,
  config: PgConfig,
  password: Secret<u8[]>,
  target: PgTarget,
): Promise<i32>
```

<scalar-field name="pool" type="PgAsyncPool" required>

The pool to fill.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="config" type="PgConfig" required>

The startup parameters and caps for the handshake.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="password" type="Secret&lt;u8[]&gt;" required>

The role's password as UTF-8 bytes; copied for each
  connection, so the caller wipes its own afterwards.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="target" type="PgTarget" required>

Where the server is, as `pgTarget` made it; a TCP host must
  be a numeric address, and a target that failed panics.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="returns" type="Promise&lt;i32&gt;">

The number of slots connected after the call.

</scalar-field>

### pgAsyncQuery

Runs one statement on the ticket's connection: Parse, Bind (each parameter
in text), Execute and Sync go out in one write, and the answer is read to
its ReadyForQuery, waiting on the socket while other tasks run. It only
reads the pool; its buffers and the answer are the calling task's.

```ts
function pgAsyncQuery(
  pool: PgAsyncPool,
  ticket: i32,
  sql: string,
  params: PgAsyncParams,
): Promise<PgAsyncResult>
```

<scalar-field name="pool" type="PgAsyncPool" required>

The pool the ticket came from.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="ticket" type="i32" required>

A ticket `pgAsyncClaim` answered and no `pgAsyncRelease` has
  spent; any other panics.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="sql" type="string" required>

One statement, `$1`, `$2`, ... naming the parameters; a NUL in
  it fails the query with `PG_ERR_ENCODING` without sending anything.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="params" type="PgAsyncParams" required>

The parameters, as many as the statement names; a NUL in
  a text one fails the query the same way.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="returns" type="Promise&lt;PgAsyncResult&gt;">

The answer; its `reusable` goes to `pgAsyncRelease`.

</scalar-field>

### pgAsyncRelease

Gives a claimed connection back, or closes it when `reusable` is false; the
ticket is spent either way, and a ticket that is not the slot's current
claim (a second release, or one after `close()`) panics. It writes only
numbers into the pool, so a spawned task may call it.

```ts
function pgAsyncRelease(
  pool: PgAsyncPool,
  ticket: i32,
  reusable: boolean,
): void
```

<scalar-field name="pool" type="PgAsyncPool" required>

The pool the ticket came from.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="ticket" type="i32" required>

The ticket `pgAsyncClaim` answered.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="reusable" type="boolean" required>

The query's `reusable`; false closes the connection.

</scalar-field>

## Classes

### PgAsyncParams

A query's parameters, in text, in the order `$1`, `$2`, ... name them. A
task builds its own; the values travel apart from the SQL, so none is ever
read as SQL.

```ts
class PgAsyncParams
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new PgAsyncParams()` | No parameters yet. |
| `readonly nulls: boolean[]` | Whether each parameter is NULL. |
| `readonly values: string[]` | Each parameter's text, `""` for a NULL. |
| `int(value: i32): void` | Adds an integer parameter, sent as its decimal text. |
| `none(): void` | Adds a NULL parameter. |
| `text(value: string): void` | Adds a text parameter. |

### PgAsyncPool

Authenticated PostgreSQL connections that spawned tasks share. Build one
and connect it with `pgAsyncConnect` outside any task; tasks then claim,
query and release through the `pgAsync*` functions, and the owner calls
`close()` once they are done. It holds no secret: only sockets and numbers.
The arrays are the functions' bookkeeping, readable for a test or a status
page; a program writes none of them.

```ts
class PgAsyncPool
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new PgAsyncPool(size: i32)` | A pool of `size` slots, none connected yet. |
| `readonly claimed: u8[]` | Each slot's state: 0 free, 1 claimed by a ticket. |
| `readonly claims: i32[]` | Each slot's claim count, the high part of its current ticket. |
| `claimWaitMs: i32` | The most milliseconds `pgAsyncClaim` sleeps waiting for a free connection before it answers `PG_CARRIER_FULL`. |
| `dropped: i32` | How many connections `pgAsyncRelease` closed rather than gave back. |
| `readonly fds: i32[]` | Each slot's socket, or -1 while it is not connected. |
| `maxColumns: i32` | The most columns a row may have; more fails the query with `PG_ERR_TOO_BIG` and closes the connection. |
| `maxMessage: i32` | The largest message a query accepts, in bytes; a larger one fails it with `PG_ERR_TOO_BIG` and closes the connection. |
| `maxRows: i32` | The most rows a query keeps; later rows are read and dropped, and the query fails with `PG_ERR_TOO_BIG`. |
| `readonly size: i32` | The number of connection slots, fixed at construction. |
| `waits: i32` | How many times `pgAsyncClaim` slept because every live connection was claimed. |
| `close(): void` | Ends every connection: a Terminate is offered to each socket, which is then closed, claimed or not. Call it once the tasks that hold tickets are done; a ticket used afterwards panics. |
| `live(): i32` | The number of slots connected now, claimed or not. |

### PgAsyncResult

One query's answer, in the task's own memory: its rows as text, its tag,
and how it ended.

```ts
class PgAsyncResult
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new PgAsyncResult()` | An answer with no rows that worked, until the query fills it in. |
| `code: i32` | `PG_CARRIER_DONE` when the query worked, `PG_CARRIER_FAILED` when it did not. |
| `columns: i32` | The number of columns in each row (the first row's; every row must match). |
| `errorCode: string` | The server's SQLSTATE when it refused the statement, e.g. `42P01`. |
| `errorMessage: string` | The server's message when it refused the statement. |
| `failure: i32` | When it failed: a `PG_ERR_*`, `PG_ERR_NONE` when the server refused the statement. |
| `readonly nulls: boolean[]` | Whether each kept cell is NULL, as `values`. |
| `reusable: boolean` | Whether the connection may serve another query: hand it to `pgAsyncRelease`. |
| `rows: i32` | The number of rows kept. |
| `socketError: i32` | When the socket failed: its negative errno, 0 when the server closed cleanly. |
| `tag: string` | The command tag, e.g. `SELECT 2` or `UPDATE 1`; `""` for an empty query. |
| `readonly values: string[]` | Every kept cell's text, row by row; `""` for a NULL. |
| `int(row: i32, column: i32, fallback: i32): i32` | A cell read as a decimal `i32`, or `fallback` when it is NULL or not one. |
| `isNull(row: i32, column: i32): boolean` | Whether a cell is NULL; panics on a row or column out of range. |
| `ok(): boolean` | Whether the query worked. |
| `text(row: i32, column: i32): string` | A cell's text, `""` for a NULL; panics on a row or column out of range. |

<scalar-card title="64" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`PG_ASYNC_MAX_SIZE: i32`

The most connections one `PgAsyncPool` holds.
